slides.say: Almost every question in this part does one of two things. It breaks a number apart into factors, or it builds numbers by multiplying pieces together.
And then it asks something simple. Which prime is missing, or which prime is there too few times? Each of these tools, we'll learn inside the question that uses it.

But first, one tool that none of the next questions uses, and the practice questions do. How many divisors does a number have? Let's take forty-four. Its divisors are one, two, four, eleven, twenty-two and forty-four. That's six.
Listing them works for small numbers. But there's a faster way, from the prime factorization. Forty-four is four times eleven, so it's two squared times eleven.

Why does this help? A divisor of forty-four is built only from its primes, twos and elevens, and never more of each than forty-four has. So a divisor chooses how many twos it takes, zero, one or two. That's three options. And how many elevens, zero or one. That's two options.
Any choice of twos goes with any choice of elevens, so I multiply the options. Three times two is six, exactly the six divisors we listed.
So the rule is, take each exponent, add one, and multiply. Why plus one? Because taking zero copies is also a choice. The divisor one, with no twos and no elevens, is that choice.

Let's see it on a bigger number, three cubed times five squared. Do I need to know what number that is? No. Listing its divisors would take a while, and the rule doesn't need it. Threes, zero to three, that's four options. Fives, zero to two, that's three options. Four times three is twelve divisors.

Now careful, the rule works only on a real prime factorization. Fifty-six is four times fourteen, and a lot of students say one plus one, times one plus one, four divisors. But four and fourteen aren't primes.
Fifty-six is two cubed times seven. So it's three plus one, times one plus one, four times two, eight divisors. One, two, four, seven, eight, fourteen, twenty-eight and fifty-six.

So, break into primes, add one to each exponent, and multiply. The factor tools card comes right after this video, and then seven questions. Try each one first, and then watch the solution. [pause] Okay. I'll see you in the next video.
